claim:
For \(0\le \xi\le1\), let
\[
X_\xi=(\mathbb R^2,N_\xi),\qquad
N_\xi(x,y)=\max\left\{|x|,|y|,\frac{|x|+|y|}{1+\xi}\right\},
\]
and let \(n(X_\xi)\) and \(n_1(X_\xi)\) denote its numerical index and rank-one numerical index. Then the multiplicative separation
\[
R(\xi)=\frac{n_1(X_\xi)}{n(X_\xi)}
\]
has a unique global maximum at
\[
\xi=\sqrt2-1.
\]
More precisely, with
\[
a=\sqrt5-2,\qquad b=\sqrt2-1,\qquad c=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2},
\]
one has \(R(\xi)=1\) on \([0,a]\cup[c,1]\), \(R\) is strictly increasing on \([a,b]\), and \(R\) is strictly decreasing on \([b,c]\). Hence
\[
\max_{0\le\xi\le1}R(\xi)
=
\frac{4}{3-\sqrt2+\sqrt{10\sqrt2-13}}
=
1.506878584864220\ldots.
\]
At the unique maximizer \(X_b\) is the regular octagonal plane,
\[
n(X_b)=\sqrt2-1,
\qquad
n_1(X_b)=
\frac{4(\sqrt2-1)}{3-\sqrt2+\sqrt{10\sqrt2-13}}
=
0.624169546700337\ldots.
\]
Thus, within this classical octagonal family, restricting the numerical-index infimum to rank-one operators loses the greatest multiplicative amount exactly at the regular octagon.

correctness.rationale: The ordinary-index and rank-one-index formulas were checked in the primary sources. Their quotient is \(1\) on the two outer parameter intervals. On the first middle interval, exact differentiation reduces the sign to \(A_-(\xi)>0\); \(P_-\) is increasing with \(P_-'(\xi)\ge12\), and \(P_-(\sqrt5-2)=16(263\sqrt5-588)>0\). On the second middle interval, exact differentiation reduces the sign to \(A_+(\xi)<0\); \(P_+\) is convex and negative at both endpoints, while the radical coefficient is also negative. These strict signs prove the unique maximizer \(\xi=\sqrt2-1\). Direct exact substitution gives the displayed radical value and identifies the maximizing norm as the regular octagon.
risks: The theorem uses the real-space normalizations in the two cited sources.
The proof concerns a ratio of two positive indices; no assertion is made outside the displayed parameter interval.

value.rationale: The rank-one numerical index was introduced precisely to compare the numerical-radius behavior of rank-one operators with that of arbitrary operators. The ratio \(n_1(X)/n(X)\) is therefore a natural dimensionless measure of the information lost by the rank-one restriction. The two cited papers supply both invariants on one canonical octagonal deformation but leave their strongest separation unquantified. The exact optimization is structurally informative: equality holds on two outer parameter regimes, the separation rises and falls strictly in the middle, and its unique peak occurs exactly at the regular octagon. This gives a complete comparison profile at the level of equality regimes and the unique worst member, rather than an arbitrary isolated parameter evaluation.
risks: The result is a structural refinement of two explicit source formulas rather than a new general theory.
Its value is tied to the natural comparison of the two numerical-index notions on a canonical family; it is not claimed as a universal extremal theorem.
